The bill changes the Customs Act 1901 so that goods from Peru, Indonesia, and Hong Kong can enter Australia with discounted import taxes.
It sets up rules for identifying which goods count as originating from each of those places and lets regulations require exporters and producers to keep records when they claim those discounts.
Budget papers say the Hong Kong deal would cost the government $40 million in lost revenue over the forecast period, while the Peru and Indonesia deals would have little or no revenue effect.
Creates rules for classifying Peruvian, Indonesian, and Hong Kong goods as eligible for lower customs duty rates.
Allows regulations to impose record-keeping duties on exporters and producers claiming preferential rates.
Works with a separate tariff bill that will list the actual reduced duty rates in the Customs Tariff Act 1995.
Australian exporters and producers of goods shipped to Peru, Indonesia, and Hong Kong, and importers of those goods into Australia.

The bill implements free trade agreements with Indonesia, Peru, and Hong Kong, aiming to increase export opportunities and reduce tariffs on Australian goods. The agreements cover 99% of Australian exports to Indonesia duty-free, new quotas for dairy and grains to Peru, and zero tariffs on all goods to Hong Kong, with support from over 30 industry groups.

The speaker argued that free trade is essential for Australia's economic prosperity and announced three free trade agreements with Indonesia, Peru, and Hong Kong, which will eliminate over 99% of tariffs on Australian goods to Indonesia and Peru and codify existing trade with Hong Kong, aiming to cover 90% of Australia's trade by free trade agreements by 2022.

Labor announced support for the Customs Amendment and Tariff Amendment bills after obtaining written commitments from Trade Minister Simon Birmingham on worker protections, including no new labour market testing waivers, criminal penalties for exploitation, and termination of the 1993 Indonesia bilateral investment treaty. The agreements are expected to boost Australian exports and jobs, with specific benefits for steel, grain, education and manufacturing sectors.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment (Growing Australian Export Opportunities Across the Asia-Pacific) Bill 2019, which enables free trade agreements with Indonesia, Hong Kong and Peru, arguing the Indonesia deal is vital given trade is 42% of GDP and Indonesia’s large market. Labor’s second reading amendment, moved by the member for Brand, sought improvements such as labour market testing, protections for working holidaymakers, replacing the 1993 investment treaty’s ISDS clause, and a review of the new clause; the trade minister agreed to most demands in a 21 October response, allowing Labor’s support.

The speaker argued that the Indonesia-Australia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (IA-CEPA) will boost trade and jobs, and announced Labor's support after securing commitments to protect Australian workers, including no additional labour testing waivers, equal treatment for visa holders, and improved investor-state dispute settlement clauses.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment (Growing Australian Export Opportunities Across the Asia-Pacific) Bill 2019 and related bills, arguing the trade agreements with Indonesia, Hong Kong, and Peru will create jobs and economic growth. The speaker cited four reasons for support: bigger markets mean more jobs, deepening ties with Indonesia is critical, improvements were negotiated on investment protections and labour standards, and engagement with Asia is needed during weak economic growth and global uncertainty.

The speaker supported the free trade agreement with Indonesia, arguing it will eliminate tariffs on grain, cattle, and steel, and create opportunities for Australian vocational education and healthcare providers, while noting that only 2% of Australian exports currently go to Indonesia.

The speaker argued that Labor supports the free trade agreements with Indonesia, Hong Kong, and Peru, citing recommendations from the Joint Standing Committee on Treaties (JSCOT) including labour market testing protections, termination of the old Indonesia bilateral investment treaty’s survival clause, and independent economic modelling. He also noted that the government should monitor Hong Kong’s autonomous status and that civil society and unions need better consultation in future trade negotiations.

The speaker argued in support of the Peru-Australia, Hong Kong, and Indonesia free trade agreements, focusing on the Indonesia-Australia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, and noted that Australia exports more to the UK than to Indonesia despite its proximity, with benefits for sectors like steel (BlueScope in Port Kembla) and education, while calling for more Indonesian language study in schools.

Labor supported the Customs Amendment bills for trade agreements with Indonesia, Hong Kong and Peru after the government agreed to demands including retaining labour market testing, modernising investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) provisions, and holding an inquiry into treaty transparency. The speaker also raised concerns about unlicensed electricians and called for stronger enforcement of workplace laws.
The speaker criticised the ignorance of MPs, noting that the previous speaker from Newcastle represents a major coalmining area while the world's biggest coalmining area is in Indonesia.

The Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills implement Australia's obligations under free trade agreements with Indonesia, Peru, and Hong Kong, eliminating over 99% of tariffs on Australian goods exports to Indonesia and Peru while guaranteeing existing duty-free access to Hong Kong. The speaker urged Parliament to pass the bills without delay to benefit Australian businesses, exporters, workers, investors, and farmers.
Customs Amendment (Growing Australian Export Opportunities Across the Asia-Pacific) Act 2019
This bill would clarify how public interest immunity applies to continuing detention order applications for terrorist offenders.

The AFP minister would have to notify a terrorist offender in writing when information is excluded from a CDO application due to public interest immunity, and the offender could then seek access to that information.
The bill states that a terrorist offender who seeks access to such information would not be required to prove to the court that the immunity claim should not be upheld.

The bill introduces a presumption against bail and parole for individuals who have supported or been linked to terrorist activities, and makes two amendments to improve the continuing detention order scheme for high-risk terrorist offenders. The measures follow a COAG agreement and recommendations from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor, with the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security unanimously recommending passage.

Labor supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment (2019 Measures No. 1) Bill 2019, which aligns with Council of Australian Governments principles from 5 October 2017 on bail and parole for terror-linked offenders and addresses a gap in continuing detention orders. The government accepted a Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security recommendation, but Labor and Liberal members disagreed on one issue relating to Australia's obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

This bill would tighten rules on unions and employer groups after a royal commission found misconduct.

New rules would also block a merger that is not in the public interest.
Include serious criminal offences as a ground for automatic disqualification from office.
Empower the Federal Court to disqualify officials who repeatedly break industrial laws or are not fit and proper.
Create an offence for a disqualified person to still act as an official.
Allow the Federal Court to cancel registration for unlawful conduct or serious criminal offences.
Expand the Federal Court's power to appoint an administrator to fix governance problems.
Introduce a public interest test for amalgamations, considering each organisation's compliance record among other things.
Registered employee and employer organisations and their officials.

The speaker moved to reject the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it attacks unions instead of addressing wage theft, stagnant wages (growing eight times slower than profits), and over 200 workplace deaths per year, and that its provisions—allowing any person of sufficient interest to disqualify officials or deregister unions—would be weaponised by employers like Liberal donor Gerry Hanssen.

The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, which would expand grounds for disqualifying union officials and make it a criminal offence for disqualified persons to hold office. The speaker cited the CFMMEU as having been fined over $16 million, with over 2,000 breaches and 74 representatives before the courts, and described alleged union intimidation and thuggery, including the physical assault of a volunteer.

The speaker argued that the government is not anti-union but opposes unions that break the law, specifically targeting the CFMMEU for over 2,000 incidents of law-breaking and $16 million in fines. He supported the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, which would make it easier for the Federal Court to deregister organisations like the CFMMEU and disqualify officials convicted of serious offences or repeated industrial law breaches.

The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is an attack on unions and workers, violating human rights and international law, and would further suppress wages—citing a 50‑year low in workers’ share of income, penalty rate cuts costing some workers up to $26,000, and total losses of $2.9 billion.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it is an obsessive government attack on unions that would suppress wages, violate international labour rights, and undermine democratic representation. They noted the bill goes beyond the Heydon royal commission recommendations, is largely unchanged from a 2017 version, and contrasts with the government's failure to establish a national anticorruption commission.

The speaker argued the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is needed to tackle illegal behaviour by unions and employer organisations, citing CFMMEU official John Setka’s 59 convictions and union intimidation during the Boothby election campaign. The bill would give courts greater powers to disqualify officials, cancel registrations, and enforce accountability for law-breaking organisations.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it allows employers or others to deregister unions and disqualify officials via a fit-and-proper-person test. He cited the government's $45 million royal commission into unions as a political attack, defended unions' role in securing wages and conditions, and referenced the Health Services Union's industrial dispute over hospital safety and ACTU president Michele O'Neil's opposition to the bill.

Repeals the medical transfer provisions in the Migration Act.
